question: Solid vs engineered hardwood: which is better on a concrete slab?
title: Solid vs Engineered Hardwood on a Concrete Slab
h1: Solid or Engineered Hardwood: Which One Handles a Slab?
description: Engineered hardwood is the better fit for slab-on-grade homes in Sarasota and Manatee counties; here's the moisture math and 2026 cost gap.
capsule: Engineered hardwood is the better choice on a concrete slab in Sarasota and Manatee counties. NWFA guidance says solid wood shouldn't go below grade, and most local homes are slab-on-grade. Engineered hardwood over a slab that tests at or below 75% relative humidity (ASTM F2170) runs about $9-$20 per sq ft installed in 2026.

sections.h2: Why solid hardwood struggles on a slab foundation
sections.html:
Most houses built in Sarasota and Manatee counties since the 1960s sit on a poured concrete slab, not a basement or a vented crawlspace. A 1,600 sq ft block ranch in Gulf Gate built in 1972 has that slab in direct contact with the ground, and groundwater vapor moves up through it every day. Solid hardwood is milled from a single piece of wood, and it moves with that moisture - swelling in the humid months, shrinking back in the dry ones. NWFA's own concrete-subfloor guidance says solid strip and plank flooring should not be installed below grade, because a slab can't be relied on to stay dry enough, long enough.

That doesn't rule out solid wood in a Sarasota home entirely - a raised, framed floor over a vented space can still take it - but on a bare slab, we steer customers toward engineered hardwood instead.

sections.h2: How engineered hardwood handles the same slab
sections.html:
Engineered hardwood is built from cross-layered plywood or high-density fiberboard with a real hardwood wear layer on top. Those cross layers resist the cupping and gapping that wrecks solid boards on a slab, so it can be glued down directly to concrete once the slab checks out. It's also thinner in most lines, which matters when a condo or a slab-to-slab transition has a tight height budget.

The tradeoff is the wear layer. A 2 mm layer is good for one or two sandings over the floor's life, 3 mm for two or three, and 4 mm for three or four - each full sanding takes off roughly 0.5-1 mm. If you want a floor that can be refinished more than once down the road, see our guide on how many times you can refinish hardwood or engineered floors and ask for the wear layer thickness in writing before you buy.

sections.h2: What the slab moisture test actually checks
sections.html: Before we quote hardwood over a slab, we run a moisture reading as part of the free estimate. The industry standard is ASTM F2170 (an in-situ relative humidity probe drilled into the slab) or ASTM F1869 (a calcium chloride test taped to the surface). NWFA's guidance sets the ceiling at 75% RH or 3 lbs per 1,000 sq ft per 24 hours, unless the installer uses a manufacturer-rated vapor-retarder system under the floor. A slab that reads above that line isn't automatically a dead end - a vapor barrier, more dry-down time, or a switch to waterproof flooring are all real options - but it changes the job and the timeline.

A slab poured in the 1970s for a Gulf Gate or Sarasota Springs ranch behaves differently than one poured last year in a Lakewood Ranch development. Older slabs have had decades to equilibrate with the water table and often read drier once any surface sealer is stripped, while a slab poured within the last year or two is still releasing the water used to mix the concrete and commonly fails a same-week moisture test. New construction almost always needs a longer dry-down period, sometimes 60-90 days past the pour, before either solid or engineered wood should go down - a detail worth asking your builder about before you schedule flooring. If your slab isn't flat as well as dry, that's a separate check we cover in our subfloor leveling service.

Nationally, HomeGuide's 2026 numbers land close to our own hardwood cost guide: solid runs $11-$25 per sq ft installed, engineered $9-$20, and a 2,000 sq ft house comes out to $14,000-$50,000 depending on wood species and pattern. The gap between solid and engineered narrows or disappears once you add the plywood subfloor solid wood needs over a slab - which is another reason most of our slab jobs end up engineered. faqs.q: Can solid hardwood ever be glued straight to a slab?
faqs.a: Most manufacturers don't warranty it. Solid wood over a slab usually needs a plywood subfloor or sleeper system first, which adds cost and height - at that point engineered on the bare slab is usually the simpler call.

faqs.q: What if my slab fails the moisture test?
faqs.a: We don't stop the job - we adjust it. Options include a rated vapor-retarder membrane, more dry-down time before install, or switching to a waterproof product like LVP that tolerates higher slab moisture.

faqs.q: Does engineered hardwood still need to acclimate before installation?
faqs.a: Yes, though generally for less time than solid wood. See our acclimation guide for how long that takes in Florida's humidity.
